name: Fraud — card-not-present checkout / transaction fraud
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.one_line_definition: A merchant, PSP, or card issuer must decide in <100 ms whether to approve, challenge, or decline an inbound e-commerce authorization or 3DS request, using per-card / per-account / per-device / per-IP behavioural features.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: Three concrete jobs: (1) Score an inbound charge / authorization within the auth-time budget (~100 ms end-to-end at Stripe Radar; the ML inference is 1–2 ms and the rest is feature collection) so the merchant or PSP can approve, step-up to 3DS, or decline. (2) Detect card-testing / BIN-attack bursts (hundreds to thousands of small auths with low amounts, shared device or IP, same expiry/CVV patterns) and short-circuit them with rate-limit / decline actions, ideally before the issuer sees the second wave. (3) Power a PSD2/PSD3 Transaction Risk Analysis (TRA) decision so a low-risk transaction can be granted an SCA exemption (fraud rate stays under the EBA reference thresholds while preserving conversion).
domain_fit.event_shapes: Typical events that would land in beava as @bv.event records: charge_attempt {ts, charge_id, card_hash, bin, last4, account_id, device_id, ip, ua_hash, billing_country, ship_country, merchant_id, mcc, amount_cents, currency, avs_result, cvv_result, is_3ds, channel}, charge_outcome {ts, charge_id, auth_decision, decline_code, processor_rt_ms}, login_attempt / session_start {ts, account_id, device_id, ip, success, mfa_used} for ATO precursors, address_change / email_change / password_reset {ts, account_id, channel} for ATO mutation signals, refund / dispute / chargeback_filed {ts, charge_id, reason_code}. Key fields are deliberately hashes/tokens (card_hash, ua_hash) so beava state contains no PAN — only stable identifiers — keeping the box out of PCI scope wherever possible.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Per-entity aggregations expressed as beava @bv.table primitives. Examples by entity: card_hash → count(charges, 1m/10m/1h/24h/7d sliding), sum(amount, 24h/7d), n_unique(merchant_id, 24h), n_unique(ip, 24h), distinct decline_code count (1h), time-since-last-decline; account_id → count(login_fail, 5m/1h), n_unique(device_id, 24h/30d), n_unique(ip_country, 24h), velocity of profile mutations (email/password/address) in 10m, max-geo-distance(login_ip_geo, 1h) for impossible-travel; device_id → n_unique(card_hash, 1h/24h), n_unique(account_id, 24h), count(charge_attempt, 5m); ip → count(charge_attempt, 1m/10m), n_unique(card_hash, 10m), share-of-declines distribution; bin → count(charge_attempt, 1m), decline-rate distribution; (card_hash, merchant_id) pair → count, time-since-first-seen. Both exact (counters, sums) and approximate (HLL for n_unique, CMS for top-K offenders) aggregates have legitimate roles — exact for the issuer's accounting-grade velocity rules, approximate for the high-cardinality device/IP fan-out.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Mixed and parallel. Primary keys in production fraud rigs include: card_hash (or PAN token), account_id / user_id, device_id (fingerprint), ip, bin, (card_hash, merchant_id) pair, (account_id, counterparty) pair, email_hash, ship_address_hash. A single decision typically reads features from 4–8 of these grains simultaneously.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: All three plus session. Sliding windows dominate (1m, 5m, 10m, 1h, 24h, 7d) because velocity rules need rolling counts; tumbling windows show up for nightly fraud-rate accounting (PSD2 TRA reference rates are quarterly tumbling); session windows show up for ATO (per login session, count mutations). Exact counts are required for regulator-facing fraud-rate accounting (PSD2 TRA) and for billing-grade chargeback liability tracking. Approximate (HLL / CMS) is acceptable and often preferred for high-cardinality device/IP n_unique features feeding the ML scorer, where a 1–2 % HLL error is invisible compared to model variance.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Mixed. The auth-time scoring path tolerates at-least-once with idempotent counters (key = charge_id), because a duplicate count of a single charge does not change the decision materially. However, the regulator-facing fraud-rate accounting for PSD2 TRA exemption eligibility, and the chargeback-liability counters, need strict no-double-count or compensating reconciliation against the system of record.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Auth-time fraud scoring runs inside a ~100 ms end-to-end budget (Stripe Radar documents this explicitly: ~1–2 ms for ML inference, leaving ~98 ms for feature collection + everything else); issuer-side 3DS ACS decisioning is also sub-100 ms. Beava's published sub-millisecond TCP get_many fits cleanly inside this budget.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to a few seconds. Card-testing bursts complete dozens to hundreds of attempts in seconds, so velocity counters that lag by even a minute are effectively useless (Tecton / Materialize / RisingWave all cite 'features stale at 5 minutes' as the failure mode that motivates real-time feature stores). Beava's push-on-event model gives single-digit-ms feature staleness.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state EPS for a mid-sized PSP or large merchant is typically 1k–20k charges/sec; large issuers and global PSPs run far higher (PayPal cited 1M TPS on Aerospike; one digital-commerce fraud system cited ~180k writes/sec + ~75k reads/sec on a 25B-record dataset). Card-testing bursts can multiply baseline by 10–100× in seconds. Beava's published 684k EPS sustained on a single Apple-M4 core (TCP+msgpack+parallel=16) sits comfortably above the single-tenant requirements of most regional PSPs and merchants but is below the largest global card networks. [uncertain] exact published EPS for Sift / Forter / Riskified production tiers.
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Balanced to slightly write-heavy: every charge attempt is one or more writes (counters tick on multiple entity grains) and typically one batched read (20–100 features). A reasonable rule of thumb is 1 batched-read per 3–5 writes; card-testing storms skew it toward write-heavy.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Order-of-magnitude per buyer: a regional PSP with ~10M active cards × ~5 entity grains (card, account, device, ip, bin) × ~30–50 features per grain × ~16 bytes per counter ≈ 24–40 GB hot state, well inside a single beava box. A global PSP with ~1B cards pushes into the hundreds of GB to low TB range and would exceed today's single-binary in-memory ceiling.
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Explosive on ip and device_id (proxy pools, botnets, residential-proxy rotation), slowly-growing on account_id and bin, bounded on merchant_id. The explosive grains are exactly the ones where HLL / CMS sketches are the right shape; the slowly-growing grains tolerate exact counters.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Mixed TTLs. Velocity counters: seconds to days (1m/10m/1h/24h/7d). Per-card behavioural profile and known-good device list: 30–90 days. Chargeback-liability accounting: 540 days+ (typical issuer chargeback window). KYC linkage data and AML-relevant flags: years. Beava's WAL+snapshot fits the seconds-to-days hot tier; the multi-year tail belongs in a different system.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20–100+ features per decision. Stripe describes 'hundreds of features' in Radar and explicitly motivates ~10× more signals per transaction with L1 caching. Real-world XGBoost/LightGBM fraud models commonly use 30–100 engineered features. Beava's batch_get / get-many path is exactly the right shape.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe is the table-stakes minimum (loss of recent velocity counters during a crash creates a brief blind spot that fraudsters can exploit). Regulator-grade durability is required for the PSD2 TRA fraud-rate accounting path and for chargeback-liability counters; those typically live in a system-of-record DB and beava's role is the hot-path aggregator. Beava's WAL + periodic snapshot + refuse-on-network-FS posture matches the crash-safe tier; for regulator-grade, beava needs to be paired with a durable downstream sink.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Single-binary regional / single-binary-per-PSP-tenant fits a regional PSP, a mid-sized merchant fraud team, or a single-issuer card programme cleanly. Multi-region active-active with strong consistency does NOT fit today: beava has no in-process sharding and no cross-region replication in v0, so a global card network with multi-region authorization paths cannot run beava as the single source of truth for velocity state without an external coordination layer.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Primarily the risk / fraud-ops team (Head of Fraud, Director of Risk) at PSPs, acquirers, card issuers, marketplaces, and large merchants; the ML platform team is a secondary buyer when the fraud team operates through it.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Large and regulator-driven. Global CNP fraud losses are projected at ~$28.1B by 2026 (40% above 2023) and ~$49B by 2030. US CNP losses reached ~$10.16B in 2024 (74% of all US card-payment fraud). The vendor TAM proxy is also large: third-party industry reports value the overall fraud-detection-and-prevention software market at ~$51–67B in 2025–2026 with 19–24% CAGRs and a path to $200B+ by the early 2030s. Specialist incumbents (Sift, Forter, Riskified, Signifyd, Featurespace, FICO Falcon, Feedzai) are well-funded and publicly visible. [uncertain] specific Sift / Forter revenue figures (private).
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: Three forces: (1) Loss curve — CNP losses growing double-digit % per year and concentrated in the buyer's P&L. (2) Regulation — PSD2 SCA already live in EU/UK, PSD3 expected 2026–2027 with stricter TRA exemption thresholds, plus FFIEC and PCI-DSS v4.0.1 retention rules. (3) Attack velocity — credential-stuffing and BIN attacks now generate thousands of attempts per hour, which makes minute-level batch features obsolete and forces fraud teams to move to streaming features whether they like it or not.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: PCI-DSS v4.0.1 — beava should never store PAN, CVV, or sensitive authentication data (SAD); buyers will demand that beava state contains only tokens / hashes / BIN to stay out of CDE scope (or, if in scope, that beava's storage / WAL / snapshot encryption story is auditable). PSD2 / PSD3 SCA + TRA — fraud-rate accounting for exemption eligibility must be exact and auditable. GDPR / CCPA — the entity grains (account_id, device_id, ip, email_hash) are personal data; retention TTLs, right-to-erasure, and data-residency apply. SOC 2 Type II is table stakes for the buyer's enterprise customers, which pushes operational requirements onto beava (TLS, auth, audit log).
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: A working per-card velocity demo (count of charges in 1m/10m/1h/24h on a card_hash with batch_get under 1 ms) can stand up in roughly a day on beava given the SDK's @bv.event / @bv.table primitives; the repo already ships a `python/beava/demos/fraud/` directory with `schema.json` and `events.jsonl`. A more realistic 30–50-feature per-card / per-device / per-IP velocity rig integrated against a real charge stream is typically a 1–2 week effort.

competition.incumbents: Two layers. (a) Generic streaming / feature-store platforms used to build fraud rigs in-house: Redis (and managed Redis on AWS / Azure / GCP), Aerospike (Barclays, PayPal public case studies), Tecton (documents a 0.8 ms feature retrieval and 100M txn/day fraud reference), Hopsworks, Feast (often on Redis), Chalk, Fennel, plus stream engines Flink, Materialize, RisingWave, Spark Structured Streaming / Spark Real-Time Mode, Confluent Flink. (b) Stateful aggregation primitives are also offered inside warehouses (Snowflake Dynamic Tables, Databricks Lakebase). Beava competes most directly with the (Redis or Aerospike) + (Flink or Materialize) two-box pattern, by collapsing it into a single binary.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Domain-specific fraud platforms that buyers would otherwise procure as black boxes: Sift, Forter, Riskified, Signifyd, Kount (Equifax), Featurespace (Visa), FICO Falcon, Feedzai, ACI, NICE Actimize, BioCatch, Sardine, Castle, SEON, Ravelin. Beava is not directly competing with these — it is the infrastructure layer a buyer would use to build or augment their own scorer, or to enrich features that get sent to one of these platforms.
competition.beava_differentiator: Five concrete differentiators: (1) Single binary — no Kafka + Flink + Redis + feature-store ETL chain; lower ops surface area for risk teams who are not data-platform teams. (2) 50+ first-class aggregation primitives covering counters, velocities, distances, rates, and distributions — exactly the shape of features fraud teams build by hand on top of Redis Lua scripts. (3) Sub-ms TCP get / batch_get fits inside the ~100 ms auth budget with margin to spare. (4) Push-on-event ingestion model (HTTP/JSON, framed TCP, msgpack) avoids the Kafka-only assumption of Tecton/Feast/Hopsworks pipelines, which matters for merchants and PSPs whose charge stream is already an HTTP webhook. (5) Apache-2.0 with no open-core split — the buyer is not negotiating against a paid 'Enterprise Edition' down the road.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: Concrete gaps that will block production CNP fraud deployments today: (1) No TLS and no auth on :8080/:8081/:8090 — for a PSP this is a non-starter even on a private subnet; auditors will block it. (2) No in-process sharding — a single global PSP's hot state cannot be split across machines; vertical scaling only. (3) No cross-region replication — multi-region active-active card programs cannot use beava as the source of truth. (4) In-memory only with refuse-on-network-FS — buyers must accept that all state is on local NVMe and a node loss requires WAL replay; regulator-grade durability needs a downstream sink. (5) No triggers / no 'fire when counter crosses threshold' — fraud teams want 'when card_hash exceeds 5 declines in 60 s, emit an action event'; today the buyer must poll. (6) No multi-tenancy / no namespace ACLs — a fraud platform vendor cannot safely host multiple merchant tenants on one beava box. (7) No secondary indexes — 'find all card_hashes with >N declines in last 10 min' is not a primary-key get and would need an out-of-band scan. (8) No native PII / token field marking — buyers running a PCI audit need an explicit posture document.
competition.integration_surface: Upstream producers in this domain are heterogeneous: Kafka (issuer-side, large PSPs), Kinesis (AWS-native shops), the merchant's own checkout webhook (HTTP push), the PSP's auth-stream gRPC, mobile SDK direct push (for device fingerprint and behavioural signals from Sardine/Castle-style SDKs), and CDC streams from Postgres/MySQL (for account-mutation events). Beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 plus framed-TCP :8081 (JSON or msgpack) maps cleanly to the webhook and mobile-SDK paths; a thin Kafka/Kinesis consumer is needed for the streaming paths and is not in v0. Downstream consumers are the ML scorer (XGBoost / LightGBM / increasingly TabTransformer-style models) and the rules engine, both pulling features via batch_get inside the auth flow.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both. The buyer typically runs (a) a rules engine for hard velocity caps and regulator-mandated decline patterns and (b) an ML scorer (XGBoost / LightGBM, increasingly transformer-based at large PSPs like Stripe) that consumes beava features. Beava is the feature substrate under both.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No publicly named beava users running this use case yet. Comparable published case studies that legitimise the shape of the problem: Barclays on Aerospike (sub-100 ms p99 at peak, 10M+ daily txns, 80% latency reduction); PayPal on Aerospike (200k → 1M TPS); Tecton fraud reference (0.8 ms feature retrieval, 100M txn/day, 40% false-positive reduction); Caulis (Redis → Aerospike fraud migration); LexisNexis (130M daily txns, 120 ms → 30 ms). Vendor reference customers for Sift / Forter / Riskified / Signifyd are extensive but private.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: [uncertain] Specific beava Discord / GitHub Discussion threads on CNP fraud — the repo ships a `python/beava/demos/fraud/` directory and a `crates/beava-bench/configs/fraud-team.json` workload, which signals fraud is a first-class internal use case, but external community traction in this domain has not been verified through this research.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: Yes. `/python/beava/demos/fraud/` contains `schema.json` and `events.jsonl`, and `/crates/beava-bench/src/workloads/fraud.rs` plus `/crates/beava-bench/configs/fraud-team.json` plus `/crates/beava-bench/tests/fraud_team_validates_against_agg_op_descriptor.rs` show that 'fraud team' is a tracked benchmark workload.
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: High / active adversary. CNP fraud is one of the most adversarial domains in computing — fraudsters adapt to detection rules within hours, rotate IPs and devices continuously, and operate distributed bots that explicitly try to stay under per-identifier velocity thresholds. Feature drift, label drift, and concept drift are all aggressive; this is the opposite of the passive-load profile of analytics or observability.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: Beava is the wrong tool for: (1) Long historical lookbacks (30–180 day per-card behavioural profiles for ML training — that belongs in a warehouse / lakehouse / offline feature store like Tecton's offline tier, Snowflake, or Databricks). (2) Full event archive for regulatory replay (PSD2 / chargeback evidentiary trails need years; beava's role is hot-path aggregation, not the system of record). (3) Cross-entity joins ('all charges in last 24h where card.bin = X AND device.country = Y AND ip.asn = Z') — beava is keyed by primary entity, not a query engine. (4) Batch model training and backfill (offline feature generation belongs in Spark/Snowflake/Databricks). (5) Long-tail KYC / AML linkage graphs (graph queries, not primary-key gets). (6) Fraud-platform vendor hosting multiple merchant tenants on one box (no multi-tenancy / namespace ACLs in v0).
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for CNP fraud at a mid-to-large buyer: (1) TLS on all three listeners (:8080, :8081, :8090) plus mTLS option. (2) AuthN/AuthZ — at minimum API-key auth scoped per namespace, ideally JWT and OIDC. (3) Triggers / event-driven actions — 'when card_hash counter crosses threshold T in window W, emit an action event to a webhook or Kafka topic' — fraud teams want push, not poll. (4) Multi-tenancy with hard namespace isolation, per-tenant quotas, and per-tenant auth (so a PSP can host multiple merchant programmes). (5) In-process sharding and consistent-hashing for entities so vertical limits do not cap a global card network. (6) Cross-region replication (active-active or active-passive with bounded staleness) for global authorization paths. (7) Approximate-aggregate primitives surfaced as first-class: HLL n_unique, CMS top-K, t-digest for amount distributions — to keep memory under control on explosive grains (IP, device). (8) Secondary indexes or scan APIs for 'find top-N entities by counter X in window W' (fraud-ops dashboards, hunter queries). (9) Configurable per-feature TTLs and eviction so 90-day per-card profiles can coexist with 1-minute velocity counters. (10) Explicit PII / token-field marking and an audit log so the buyer can pass PCI-DSS v4.0.1 and SOC 2 audits without manual evidence collection. (11) A durable downstream sink (Kafka / S3 / Postgres CDC out) so regulator-facing fraud-rate accounting can be reconciled against a system of record. (12) Rate-of-change and percentile aggregation primitives (already partly covered by the '50+ primitives' claim but worth verifying against the explicit list of velocity / distance / distribution operators).
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes, materially. CNP fraud is one of the strongest pulls for the trigger/action gap — fraud teams want 'when counter crosses threshold, emit action' as a primitive, not 'poll every N ms and act if you see it.' Card-testing bursts in particular are mitigated by sub-second triggers (auto-rate-limit the BIN or IP for 60 s) and today beava cannot do this natively.
